chunk_findings.detail: The new cap can make a loaded run receive a *shorter* timeout than the declared/idle run, worsening the bug it is meant to fix. For example, set `[gates].max_run_timeout_s = 3000`, `declared_s = 3600`, `workers.inputs["max"] = 48`, and `workers.n = 24`. An idle run (`workers.n == 48`) returns `3600`, but the loaded run computes `min(3000, int(3600 * 48 / 24)) == 3000`. The gate is therefore killed 600 seconds earlier under load than on an idle host, exactly the “timed out before baseline-red can be reached” failure mode.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/workers.py:timeout_for`

chunk_findings.detail: The added regression tests do not exercise the actual gate-runner path that caused B2efda94671; they only call `WK.timeout_for` directly. If the new line in `ddflow/services/gates/runner.py` (`timeout_s = WK.timeout_for(...)`) were removed or reverted, all four new tests would still pass, so the regression test does not protect the fix. A test is needed that runs a command gate with a loaded-host `Workers` result (or a fake `CommandRunner`) and asserts the subprocess receives the scaled timeout.
chunk_findings.title: `tests/test_auto_workers.py:138`

chunk_findings.detail: The added test uses `_run_cut(cfg(hi=48))`, where load=1.5 cuts the 48-ceiling to 32 workers, not to <=8. Therefore `WK.timeout_for(3600, cut, c)` computes `min(21600, int(3600 * 48 / 32)) = 5400`, not the asserted `21600`. chunk_findings.detail: The new guard makes `gates.max_run_timeout_s` non-binding whenever it is set below the declared timeout. With `declared_s=3600`, `[gates].max_run_timeout_s=3000`, `hi=48`, and `workers.n=24`, the returned value is `max(3600, min(3000, 7200)) == 3600`, even though the configured maximum is 3000. The prior implementation returned 3000 in this same loaded scenario, so this change removes the only branch that honored a low cap: an operator cannot use this knob to force a 3000s stop for a loaded gate, and the gate will run for 3600s.

data.probe: max_run_timeout_s bounds a per-run OVERRIDE (a larger --timeout is refused), NEVER the DECLARED gate timeout (3600), so a declared 3600s run is a legitimate budget the scaling must not cut; the guard keeps the loaded run at its declared budget, never less. A low cap does not, and never did, reduce a declared gate timeout -- it only refuses a larger override.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard can make `timeout_for` return a timeout above the configured `[gates].max_run_timeout_s`. For example, with `cfg.gates.max_run_timeout_s = 3000`, `declared_s = 3600`, `workers.inputs["max"] = 48`, and `workers.n = 24`, the code computes `cap = 3000`, `scaled = int(3600 * 48 / 24) = 7200`, and returns `max(3600, min(3000, 7200)) = 3600`. Thus the loaded gate is allowed to run for 3600 seconds even though the operator configured a maximum run timeout of 3000 seconds; the previous code returned `3000` for this input. As written, the named maximum is not a maximum when it is below `declared_s`, which violates the bounded-stop expectation in [r-bounded-everything].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workers.py:151

chunk_findings.detail: When `[gates].max_run_timeout_s` is unset (the default), `cap = int(cfg.gates.max_run_timeout_s or declared_s)` makes `cap == declared_s`. For a loaded host, e.g. `declared_s = 3600`, `workers.inputs["max"] = 48`, `workers.n = 24`, `scaled = int(3600 * 48 / 24) = 7200`, so `min(cap, scaled) = 3600` and `max(declared_s, 3600) = 3600`. This is exactly the `--timeout 3600` scenario in B2efda94671, so the gate still receives 3600s under load and the fix does not repair the reported default configuration; scaling only changes anything when `max_run_timeout_s` is explicitly greater than `declared_s`.
